Battle of Actium. In 31 BC, off the coast of northwestern Greece, Octavian defeated the combined naval forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII, and in doing so became history's first emperor.

The battle took place in the waters off Actium, where Octavian commanded around 400 warships under his admiral Agrippa, while Antony and Cleopatra mustered approximately 500 vessels. Despite their superior numbers, Antony's fleet was seriously weakened. Supply problems plagued his forces, desertions ate away at his strength, and many of his Egyptian contingents proved unreliable.

Agrippa's tactical skill made the difference. His superior command and the better ship handling of Octavian's crews allowed them to win several key engagements and eventually break through Antony's center. The Egyptians and their allies soon lost heart. Antony and Cleopatra fled to Egypt, and their remaining allies surrendered to Octavian.

As Octavian closed in on Egypt, the two leaders chose death over capture. Both committed suicide. With them went the last obstacle to Octavian's absolute power.

The battle did far more than decide a civil war. It effectively ended the Roman Republic itself and inaugurated the Principate, an era of imperial rule that would last five centuries. Octavian, who took the title Augustus, had become the master of Rome and the known world. Among his former rivals, Octavian had once been Mark Antony's triumviral colleague, and the Egyptian queen Cleopatra had sealed her fate by choosing Antony's side. What Actium created was the Roman Empire itself.
